source: Fan, Cheng, Li, Liang, Zhou, Feizi (2026) Thinking Hard, Not Smart: Reasoning Models Fail to Ration Test-Time Compute Across Questions
finding: Exam-style test: N Omni-MATH questions with visible point values share one token budget. Seven reasoning models (five open, two DeepSeek-V4) act as greedy sequential solvers. They follow presentation order, front-load effort and ignore point value. A planning prompt spreads compute but does not make it value- or difficulty-aware.
numbers: Effort vs position correlation -0.34 overall (-0.17 at N=5, -0.38 at N=10, -0.48 at N=20). Solving order vs position +0.68. Effort vs difficulty +0.33/+0.26/+0.11 for N=5/10/20 (reactive, not prospective). Effort vs point value 0.00/+0.04/+0.11. Open-model coverage falls from 80% to 40% (N=5 to N=20); DSV4-F reaches 23% at N=20. Zero-token rate at N=20: 51% open average, 69% DSV4-F. Questions the model could not solve took 24% of the work set and 32% of tokens. Planning prompt lifted DSV4-F coverage 0.23 to 0.33 but open-model order-position correlation only moved 0.64 to 0.60. Shared budget beat an equal split by 2.6 points at N=5 and lost by 5.0 points at N=20.
quote: Current models know how to think hard about the question in front of them, but not how to decide which question is worth thinking about.
limits: Omni-MATH is the only full factorial design; CRUXEval-O has two exam lengths and four models. No explicitly budget-trained model was tested. Same direction as R3-Bench (a28) but a different design, so a second independent source for K15.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: a prompt asking the model to plan its budget does not fix priorities. The allocator should sit in the scaffold: rank items by estimated value per cost before solving, and cap each item. Hard-first order breaks sequential play, so S0 must not rely on presentation order.

source: Zhao, Tian, Qi, Sun (2026) ROI-Reasoning: Rational Optimization for Inference via Pre-Computation Meta-Cognition
finding: Trained a 1.5B model to predict a cost level per problem and to solve-or-skip under one shared token budget (stage 1 fine-tuning, stage 2 RL). It beats training-free planners and larger models. Frontier size does not predict allocation skill. Training-free TALE-EP and Plan-and-Budget baselines were inconsistent in math but helped in MCQA and code.
numbers: Three-problem test papers, max score 3. Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct base: Hard-512 score 0.15, regret 0.73. TALE-EP Hard-512: 0.18, regret 0.53. ROI-Reasoning Hard-512: 0.93, regret 0.14; Medium-512 0.97 vs base 0.33. GPT-4o-mini Hard-512 0.32; DeepSeek-V3.2 (685B) 0.49. Plan-and-Solve lowered the base score (Medium-512 0.15 vs 0.33). Code Hard-256: ROI +306% over Plan-and-Budget (0.18 to 0.73). Abstract claims up to +417% over the strongest same-backbone baseline in math.
limits: Tiny setting: three problems per paper, 1.5B backbone, trained on the same budget it is tested on (with some transfer to other lengths in Table 4). Regret is measured against an easy-to-hard reference order, not a true oracle. Needs weights, so only the idea transfers.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: shows a shared-budget allocator can close much of the gap, but the gain came from training a cost predictor plus a skip option. For a no-training scaffold, the transferable parts are the cost-level tag and the explicit skip decision, to be tested per domain.

source: Cuadron et al. (2025) The Danger of Overthinking: Examining the Reasoning-Action Dilemma in Agentic Tasks
finding: On SWE-bench Verified agent runs, higher overthinking scores (favouring internal reasoning over acting on feedback) go with lower issue resolution. Reasoning models score nearly three times higher on overthinking. Picking the lower-overthinking of two low-effort runs nearly matches one high-effort run at lower cost.
numbers: 19 models; about 3,908 trajectories scored in the body (abstract says 4018). Overthinking score 0-10 from an LLM judge (Claude Sonnet 3.5), validated against human experts. o1 low-effort runs had 35% higher overthinking than high-effort runs. Lowest-Overthinking@2 from low-effort o1: 27.3% resolved at about $800 vs 29.1% for high effort at $1,400 (43% cheaper). With 3 samples: 30.3% vs 29.1%, still $200 cheaper.
limits: One task family (software engineering). The overthinking score is judged by another LLM after the run, so it is not a cheap online gate. Low reasoning effort raised overthinking, so less thinking is not automatically better in agent loops.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: early-exit gains do not carry over as a plain 'think less' rule in agentic work. What to cap is private simulation instead of acting. S0 for agent steps should favour a cheap action that returns feedback over a longer private chain, and the scaffold can choose between two cheap runs using a behaviour score.

source: Fu, Wang, Tian, Zhao (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Local (lowest group) confidence of each reasoning trace is used to drop weak traces online and to stop sampling when votes agree. No training. Needs a warm-up of 16 full traces per prompt to set a threshold; the warm-up counts toward cost in their budget.
numbers: Budget K=512 traces, 4,096-trace pool, 64 repeats. Online DeepConf-low cuts tokens 43-79% vs majority voting on AIME24/25, BRUMO25, HMMT25; DeepConf-high cuts 18-59%. DeepSeek-8B mean savings 62.88% (low) and 47.67% (high). Accuracy: +5.8 on AIME24 (DeepSeek-8B), -0.9 on BRUMO25 (Qwen3-32B). Offline top-10% filter helped in 12 of 20 settings (+0.26 to +9.38) and hurt in 8 (-0.31 to -4.69), mean +1.22.
limits: Math contests only. Needs token log-probs. The authors name confidently wrong traces as a key limitation. Baseline is a 512-sample vote, a very expensive reference, so savings are relative to a large fixed budget.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: a confidence-and-consensus stopping rule saves most tokens against a fixed large-N vote, but the warm-up (16 traces) is a fixed gate cost that is small only when the reference N is large. For a scaffold with N around 5-8 the warm-up would eat the savings.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Know When They're Right: Probing Hidden States for Self-Verification
finding: A small probe on hidden states predicts whether an intermediate answer is correct, with good calibration. Used as an early-exit gate it cuts tokens at no accuracy loss. It does not transfer across domains (logic to math), and degrades for short-CoT models.
numbers: ROC-AUC above 0.7 and ECE below 0.1 in distribution (R1-distill models; GSM8K, MATH, AIME, KnowLogic 5.4k multiple choice). Threshold 0.85: 88.2% accuracy (same as no early exit) with about 24% fewer tokens; threshold 0.9: 88.6% accuracy, 19% fewer tokens. At matched tokens the probe beat static early exit by up to 5 points (87.4% at threshold 0.8 vs about 82.5%).
limits: Needs hidden-state access and per-domain training data. The probe does not stably generalise from logical to math reasoning. Probes trained on easier math sets were less calibrated on AIME.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: a cheap learned confidence gate works inside a domain but is not a drop-in for mixed tasks. A black-box scaffold cannot use hidden states, so it needs verbalised or consistency-based confidence, which this paper does not test.

source: Han et al. (2025) Token-Budget-Aware LLM Reasoning (TALE)
finding: Putting a token budget in the prompt can cut output length, but if the budget is set too low, actual tokens go up (token elasticity). A zero-shot estimator (the model itself) guesses a budget, then a second prompt includes it. The estimate lands in the ideal range about 61% of the time.
numbers: Across 7 datasets TALE-EP: 81.03% accuracy vs 83.75% for vanilla CoT, tokens 32% and expense 41% of vanilla. Four models on MathBench-College: tokens down 64.63% on average, expense down 45.30%; accuracy 76.67% (Yi-lightning), 70.00% (GPT-4o-mini), 80.00% (GPT-4o). Estimated budget in the ideal range 60.61% of the time; out-of-range misses average 109.64 tokens. Scaling the estimate x2 on Llama-3.1-8B GSM8K-Zero: accuracy 67.33% to 72.66%, tokens 210.97 to 279.78. Open-ended tasks (code summary, empathetic reply, code generation): about 40% of the tokens at comparable BLEU. Budget search for training data took about 354 minutes on an A100 for 7,473 GSM8K items.
limits: TALE-EP adds a second query per item; the appendix on end-to-end latency was cut off in the text I could extract, so the net latency saving is not confirmed here. Elasticity is shown on GPT-4o-mini and Yi-lightning only.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: a prompt-only budget does work, but only in a band. The safe design is an estimate with a multiplier above the minimum, never the minimum. The elasticity point for our model must be measured: sweep budgets and look for the turn where tokens rise.

source: Callaway, Van Opheusden, Gul, Das, Krueger, Lieder, Griffiths (2022; preprint 2021) Rational use of cognitive resources in human planning (PsyArXiv byaqd; Nature Human Behaviour)
finding: Four mouse-tracing planning experiments (Mouselab-style). People plan close to a cost-sensitive optimal model and adapt search order and stopping to the environment, but with systematic departures. The figures 86% of the best trade-off and 55% strategy agreement do not appear in this paper.
numbers: Exp 1: 104 recruited, 95 analysed (Prolific). Exp 2: 313 recruited, 298 analysed. Exp 3: 319 recruited, 291 analysed. Exp 4: 137 recruited, 93 analysed (37 did not finish). Aim was 100 per condition, no formal power analysis. Exp 1: people earned 0.92 points less than the best possible at the same click count and 4.94 more than random clicking (95% CI 4.43-5.44, Wilcoxon z=8.40). They expanded a maximal-expected-value path 81.5% of the time (95% CI 79.6-83.3). 45 participants were best fit by the optimal model, 41 by a best-first variant, 9 by something else. Exp 4: forward search violated 7.2% of the time. Backward planning when variance rises with depth, as predicted, but a depth-two bias the model did not predict.
limits: Same lab as the model. Deterministic environments only. Pre-registered, with deviations listed in the SI. Cost parameters are fit per participant. Mapping of the 319-person sample to Exp 3 is inferred from the methods order.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: answered for the primary paper. The 86% and 55% figures in K05 should be dropped or re-sourced; use the real numbers (0.92 points under the Pareto front, 81.5% best-first, 45 vs 41 best fit). Best-first expansion is near-optimal at a given cost, so a scaffold can use best-first expansion with a cost-based stop.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Sleep-time Compute: Beyond Inference Scaling at Test-time
finding: Pre-processing a shared context offline pays back only when queries are related to the context. The benefit shrinks when there are few questions per context or when the query is hard to predict from the context.
numbers: Total cost modelled with test-time tokens weighted 10x sleep-time tokens. With 10 questions per context, average cost per query falls by up to 2.5x. With few questions per context sleep-time is less favourable in total cost (Fig 9). In five predictability bins, the accuracy gap between sleep-time and plain test-time compute widens as predictability rises. Scaling sleep-time compute lifts accuracy by up to 13% at similar test-time budget (Stateful GSM-Symbolic) and up to 18% on Stateful AIME. A context-only guessing baseline confirms queries are not trivially guessable.
limits: Synthetic splits of math problems into context plus question (GSM-Symbolic, AIME); the 10x latency weight is an assumption. The multi-query set was generated by o3-mini. Authors say unpredictable queries may be better served by standard test-time compute.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: offline precomputation pays when many queries share a context and are predictable. For wide-ranging queries on one context it does not. In our scaffold, cache only what several later steps will reuse (a problem restatement, a decomposition), not per-query reasoning.

source: Manvi, Singh, Ermon (2024) Adaptive Inference-Time Compute: LLMs Can Predict if They Can Do Better, Even Mid-Generation
finding: A fine-tuned Llama 3.1 8B answers a one-token question ('would you do better if you started over?') mid-generation. That one-token gate decides whether to draw more samples or to prune weak ones. It was tested on open-ended chat (AlpacaEval) as well as GSM8K.
numbers: Best-of-16 win rate vs GPT-4 on AlpacaEval 21% to 34% (33.8% with token-prediction self-evaluation); GSM8K 84.2% to 91%. Adaptive sampling got 74% of the 16-sample improvement with 1.2 samples on average (with temperature annealing). Pruning 75% of 16 samples after 128 tokens cut tokens per prompt from 7,259 to 3,220. Training set about 30,000 on-policy preferences from LMSYS prompts, ties about 40% of the time.
limits: Needs fine-tuning on the model's own outputs; the gate is trained on the model it gates. Llama 3.1 70B reaches 38.1% (AlpacaEval) and 95.1% (GSM8K) as a reference. The gate costs one token per check only because it is a trained single-token head.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 3: a cheap self-assessment gate has been shown on open-ended chat, not only math, but only after training. A zero-shot version of the same question is the prompt-only test to run on our model, with its own overhead counted.

source: Aggarwal, Madaan, Yang, Mausam (2023) Let's Sample Step by Step: Adaptive-Consistency for Efficient Reasoning and Coding with LLMs
finding: Bayesian (Beta) stopping rule on answer counts, compared with other stopping rules at the same sampling cost. Beta beat entropy and majority-threshold rules, tied Dirichlet and CRP, and was far cheaper to compute. Covers non-math sets (StrategyQA, date understanding, snarks, ruin names, salient translation, logic, coding).
numbers: 17 datasets, 3 LLMs, up to 40 samples (more for coding). Average 3.3 fewer samples with under 0.1% accuracy drop (0.04% on the headline plot); 2-4x range; Vicuna-13B 1.9 fewer, GPT-3.5-Turbo 4.4 fewer with under 0.2% drop. At equal sampling cost accuracy up to 5 points higher than self-consistency. Stopping-rule compute: Beta 0.03 ms, four orders of magnitude faster than the other variants. On GSM-8K Beta beats Entropy and Majority at 4-18 generations.
limits: Only vote counts are used, so it cannot stop a single long chain. Needs several sampled answers, so it is a parallel rule. Old models (GPT-3.5, Vicuna, 2023); no comparison with confidence-probe rules in the same paper.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 10: the stopping computation is free; the cost is the samples. No paper I opened compares Adaptive-Consistency, DEER and a value-of-computation threshold at equal tokens, so the choice must be tested on our tasks.

source: Yang et al. (2025) Dynamic Early Exit in Reasoning Models (DEER)
finding: Training-free: at each thought switch, force a trial answer and exit if its token confidence exceeds a threshold. Works on 11 reasoning models and 10 benchmarks (math, science incl. GPQA-Diamond, code). The trial answer adds latency, so the token saving is larger than the time saving. Prompt-level token budgets fail on hard items.
numbers: Latency down 27.9% to 40.1% for original DEER, 36.3% to 58.6% with branch-parallel decoding (their Fig 7). On QwQ-32B, where most baselines fail because of broken end-of-thinking markers, DEER still cut length 19.1%. Robust for confidence threshold 0.9-0.97; a threshold too low gives a large accuracy drop, too high gives late exit. Token-budget prompting 'fails on complex problems (such as AIME24)' where models write longer than vanilla CoT.
limits: Only the trial-answer overhead is acknowledged in prose; no net token count including trial answers in the part I read. Needs token probabilities. Longest trial answers are in code.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4, 5 and 10: confirms probe overhead is real (latency saving below token saving) and that a plain prompt budget breaks on hard items. A scaffold using a trial-answer probe should count the trial tokens inside the budget.

source: Liu et al. (2026) Budget-Aware Tool Use Enables Effective Agent Scaling (Budget Tracker, BATS)
finding: Agents with a plain tool-call budget plateau because they do not know the budget. A prompt-level Budget Tracker (continuous budget display) lets them use a small budget as well as a large one, and BATS adds budget-conditioned verification (SUCCESS, CONTINUE, PIVOT). Training-free; tested on web search agents and software-engineering agents.
numbers: Gemini-2.5-Pro on BrowseComp: ReAct with 100 tool calls 12.6%; Budget Tracker with 10 calls 12.8% with 40.4% fewer search calls and 31.3% lower cost. BATS at 100 tool uses: 24.6% BrowseComp, 46.0% BrowseComp-ZH, 27.0% HLE-Search. Verification retries add 5.9 points (18.7% to 24.6%). Software engineering at budget 50: resolve rate 55.4% vs 36.8% baseline at similar calls (45.7 vs 46.0) and cost (18.88 vs 18.50); Budget Tracker at 50 beat the baseline at 60 (55.4% vs 53.2%) with 9.9% fewer calls.
limits: Gemini-family agents, search and SWE tasks; BrowseComp accuracy is low (12-25%), so differences rest on small bases. The baseline resolve rate jumps from 36.8% (budget 50) to 53.2% (budget 60), so SWE comparisons are noisy. Authors' own system.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3, 5 and 6: a prompt-only budget display avoids the backfire seen with a tiny token cap, and the gain holds on agentic tasks. Cheap to copy into the scaffold: show remaining budget at each step.

source: Lieder, Griffiths, Huys, Goodman (2018) Empirical evidence for resource-rational anchoring and adjustment (Psychonomic Bulletin and Review)
finding: Time cost and error cost were varied independently in an estimation task with controlled knowledge. Adjustment fell as time cost rose and rose as error cost rose, for self-generated and provided anchors. This is the experimental test of the anchoring model, and it manipulates the costs rather than fitting them afterwards.
numbers: Two experiments; sample sizes not in the abstract page I read.
limits: Abstract only (Europe PMC); full text and sample sizes not opened. Same lab as the model. Still no independent replication found.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: costs can be manipulated and so set from outside the model; a scaffold can set time and error prices as explicit parameters and test the predicted direction instead of fitting afterwards.

source: Xie and Moss (2025) Task representation and individual differences affect strategy selection and problem-solving performance (Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: A direct replication of an earlier experiment testing the RCCL theory of strategy selection (Building Sticks Task). All four prior findings replicated, including that people prefer strategies with higher base rates of success. This replicates a related, non-Lieder strategy-selection result, not Lieder and Griffiths.
numbers: N=144 participants, plus three individual-difference tasks.
limits: Abstract only (Europe PMC). Tests success-rate learning, not the cost term of resource-rationality. Not an independent test of Lieder and Griffiths 2017.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: the nearest replication found. It supports 'strategy choice follows learned success rates' but does not test cost sensitivity. K02 stays single-source for the cost part.

source: Vul, Goodman, Griffiths, Tenenbaum (2014) One and done? Optimal decisions from very few samples; Sanborn, Zhu, Spicer, Chater (2020) Sampling as a resource-rational constraint (BBS); Zhu et al. (2024) Autocorrelated Bayesian Sampler
finding: Vul et al. derive that very few samples are globally optimal when sampling costs time. A Warwick group (Sanborn, Zhu, Chater) independently builds on sampling as the key constraint, but argues that resource-rationality cannot settle what the constraints are. Their 2024 sampler model explains probability judgments, confidence and response times with autocorrelated samples.
limits: Abstract-level read through Europe PMC. These are model papers, not replications. The 2020 commentary supports the critic view in K17.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: independent groups use and extend the sampling result, which makes K03 more than a single-lab idea, but nobody has run a direct replication of the cost-sensitive behavioural results.

source: Wu, Wang, Ye, Du, Jegelka, Wang (2025) When More is Less: Understanding Chain-of-Thought Length in LLMs
finding: Accuracy follows an inverted U with CoT length. The best length grows with task difficulty and shrinks as models get more capable. Length-aware filtering at inference helps. This gives a model-specific optimum to measure.
numbers: Abstract and intro only read this session; no figures recorded.
limits: Read only the abstract and first page, so numbers are not extracted. Mostly math with trained models.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: supports a per-model sweep of budget to find the turn point; a stronger model needs a shorter chain, so reuse of a budget across models is unsafe.
